prime.problem: Messages, webhooks and timers arrive whenever they like, but a session can only take one change at a time. Without a part of the system that owns the session, two runs write the same transcript, a redelivered message triggers a second run, and a mid-run correction is either ignored or cuts into a running tool.
prime.fits: First card of the Runs course. The agent loop showed what happens inside one turn; this card is the layer that decides which turn runs, on which session, and when. The next card (retry, replay, resume) is the runtime underneath it.
expect: one writer per session + global throttle
busy policy: collect, followup, steer, interrupt
prime.goal: Trace any burst of inbound messages through the control plane and say, for each one, which invariant handles it and when it reaches the model under each busy policy.

attend: Why does one writer per session need a separate global cap, when each session is already serialized?
In the Tuesday timeline, which invariant stops the 14.0 s redelivery, and what would happen to it if only debounce existed?
Under steer, why does the correction wait until pytest finishes instead of landing at 11.8 s?
Why does Hermes treat SQLite's one-writer rule and the gateway's one-active-turn rule as two different things?
If you ran two gateway processes behind a load balancer, which guarantee on this card would you stop trusting first?

must: One run per session lane → a correction can't start a parallel run on the same transcript → no interleaved tool calls or duplicate sends → but now something must decide when the waiting message gets in (the busy policy)

Busy policy is a setting, not model behaviour → collect/followup wait for the run to end (correction lands after the damage) → interrupt aborts at once (preempts inside a tool call) → steer checks after each tool call and skips the rest of that message's calls (safe boundary, small delay)

Real channels redeliver and humans type in bursts → dedupe on (channel, peer, session, message id) drops repeats and debounce merges a burst into one turn → each human intent becomes exactly one queued turn → fewer surprise runs

Serialization covers one session's history only → two sessions, non-idempotent tools and stale assumptions are untouched → idempotency keys on side effects and a global cap are separate guarantees, and none of them makes a 'Done' true
elevated: OpenClaw's queue is small and in-process → its one-writer guarantee is (my reading) process-local → run two gateway processes and the lane no longer stops two writers; that is the distributed lease problem behind Hermes issue #83736
reference: the five queue mode names and which one is default (collect)
Hermes key shapes like agent:main:telegram:dm:… and the state.db location
the illustrative timings (10.0 s, 10.8 s, 11.8 s, 13.0 s, 14.0 s, 30.0 s) and 1.0 s debounce window

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the path an inbound message takes from the channel to the agent loop, naming each box, then write two sentences on what the busy policy decides and why steer is the middle option.
checklist: dedupe → debounce → resolve session key → session lane (one writer) → global lane (cap) → runtime
the control plane decides what the run is; the runtime decides how the turn proceeds
busy policy decides when a queued message reaches the model: after the run, at the next tool boundary, or by aborting
steer avoids both ignoring the correction and preempting inside a tool call
idempotency keys protect retried side effects; serialization alone does not

retrieve.q: Explain why a session is an isolation boundary and not just chat history, using the user-ID-as-session-key failure.
answer: a session is where writes commit in one order and scratch state stays separate
one user can have many sessions, so keying by user ID merges unrelated tasks
they then share transcript and scratch state and the system looks fine until it acts wrongly

retrieve.q: Walk the three Slack deliveries of the Tuesday example (10.0 s, 10.8 s, 14.0 s) through the control plane under steer. When does the model see the correction, and what tool call doesn't run?
answer: 10.0 and 10.8 are new ids and 0.8 s apart → debounced into one turn, ready at 11.8 s
the session lane is busy, so no second run; steer waits for the current tool call
pytest ends at 13.0 s → queue checked → the test-file edit is skipped → correction injected before the next reply
the 14.0 s redelivery has the same message id → dropped by dedupe

retrieve.q: You run a support agent where a duplicated refund is costly and corrections are rare. Pick a busy policy and name the extra guarantee you still need.
answer: collect or followup: deterministic, the run finishes as planned before reading new input
or steer if corrections must stop a planned action, accepting a wait until the tool boundary
avoid interrupt: aborting mid-tool can leave a refund half-done
regardless: an idempotency key on the refund call, because one writer per session doesn't stop a retried side effect

retrieve.q: Hermes's SQLite store already allows only one writer at a time. Why does the gateway still need its own one-active-turn rule?
answer: the database rule is per write; a turn is many writes
two turns could alternate writes and both be 'valid' to SQLite
the semantic rule is about who owns the conversation, not storage locking

compare.q: The agent loop card owned the loop from one request to 'Done'. What does that card silently assume that this card makes explicit, and how does each fail when the assumption breaks?
answer: the loop assumes one caller and a conversation nobody else writes to
the control plane enforces that: one run per session, ordered inbound events
the loop fails inside a turn (bad stop reason, budget); the control plane fails between turns (two writers, duplicate run, lost correction)

compare.q: Dedupe on message id and idempotency keys on side effects both make 'the same thing twice' happen once. What is fundamentally different about where each sits and what it protects?
answer: dedupe sits at the door and protects against a second run being started
idempotency keys sit at the side effect and protect against a retried action in the world
a run can be correctly single and still retry a send, so you need both
durable execution adds the runtime's view: replaying a step must not redo its effect

predict.q: Keep the Tuesday timeline but shrink the debounce window to 0.5 s (the two messages are 0.8 s apart). Under steer, how many separate turns get queued, when does the model first see a correction, and does the test edit still get skipped?
predict.answer: Two turns: 0.8 s is longer than the window, so m1 flushes alone at 10.5 s and m2 at 11.3 s. Both are queued before pytest ends at 13.0 s, so steer still checks at 13.0 s, skips the test edit and injects what is waiting. The first correction still reaches the model at 13.0 s. What changes is message boundaries: the model gets two queued messages instead of one merged turn, and under followup they could become two follow-up turns.
